newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr seizes 100 yen as rate fears fade.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr seizes 100 yen as rate fears fade.

text.p: The Australian dollar rose across the board Thursday after disturbingly strong domestic wage data made it far less likely official rates would be cut soon.

The closely watched measure on average weekly ordinary time earnings showed annual growth surged to 4.6 percent in Q1 from 3.9 percent, putting it inside the Reserve Bank's danger zone of 4.5-5.0 percent and so arguing against an imminent easing.

Money market rates shot higher in response to restore the dollar's appeal as a haven for offshore funds, particularly for Japan where demand was sharp enough to pierce the magical one yen to one cent barrier for the first time since May 1992.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the dollar had leapt to US$0.7847/52, its best local close in three weeks, from an early US$0.7808/13 and US$0.7813/18 late here Wednesday.

Traders emphasised the going had been far from easy with the market made wary by rumours of big sell orders, in part from a local bank which took out a truck load of call options last week related to the purchase of a Victorian state power station.

A well known Swiss name added to the caution by selling in serious amounts atop US$0.7850, but dealers expected Europe to take it toward chart resistance at US$0.7895 tonight once it realised how far rates had swung in its favour.

Expectations of another U.S. hike by the Federal Reserve and the lingering chance of an easing here had seen spreads between U.S. and Australian bonds contract sharply and even turn negative at the short end.

Everything changed this week as benign U.S. employment cost data made the market reassess its expectations for how much the Federal Reserve would have to tighten this year -- so much so that it shrugged off a whopping 5.6 percent rise in Q1 U.S. GDP reported on Wednesday.
In contrast today's Australian wage figures were just as emphatic on the upside as the U.S. data were well behaved.
The 1.3 percent rise in weekly earnings was the biggest gain since Q2 1995 and topped even the highest market forecast.

There were also signs of strength outside the full-time adult sector since total earnings for all employees, including part-time, leapt 1.7 percent in the qaurter taking annual growth to 3.8 percent from just 2.8 percent in Q4.

Analysts cautioned the strength may have been concentrated in the state sector so lessening the inflationary implications, but the breakdown between private and public would not be released until May 22. In the meantime it would be hard for the Reserve Bank to ease policy after its board meeting next week.
"It must be a real concern to the policy makers that we are getting such wage outcomes when the labour market is so weak, said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
Jobs data so far this year had been been a lot softer than expected and were the main cause of recent specuation the RBA might ease again.

"Obviously, there's more to interest rates than wages, but they get a big weighting and these sorts of figures are a concern," he said, adding it was now very unlikely the bank would move at its monthly board meeting next Tuesday.
The money market seemed to agree and pushed rates higher.
The June bank bill future sank nine basis points to 94.0, exactly matching the current 6.0 percent cash rate.

The lift in yields attracted Japanese demand both for Australian government bonds and yen/A$ dual currency samurais and chased the dollar to a five year high of 100.02/12 yen from 99.15/25 late Wednesday. In trade weighted terms it shot to 61.1 from a previous 60.7 close.
More upbeat data was expected Friday when first quarter real retail sales were seen rising a chunky 2.4 percent, adding around 0.5 point to GDP growth for the quarter.
